# Automation and Workforce Transition Roadmap — Warehouse Network

**Paper for the Operations and Capital Committee — Revision 2**
**Sanction requested: Stage 1 only (€6.9m). Stages 2 and 3 return to this committee at named gates.**

---

### How this revision was prepared

Revision 1 was, quite properly, sent back. It set out a way of thinking about the problem and did not answer the four questions the committee actually asked. This revision answers all four, and in doing so accepts several challenges that were put to us — most importantly on the treatment of our largest site, where the earlier draft substituted a sentiment for a plan. We are grateful for the correction and have reversed the position; the reasoning is set out openly in §7 rather than quietly amended.

The work was done with the five site general managers over four sessions, with HR on tenure and attrition records, with Finance on the baseline and the hurdle test, and with Internal Audit on what can and cannot be attested. Where the group has reached a shared view, the paper says so. Where views still differ — and on two matters they do — the difference is recorded rather than smoothed over, so that the committee decides with the same information the working group has.

**Stated assumptions.** All five sites operate in a single euro-area jurisdiction. Works councils are in place at Site 1 (Halverton) and Site 3 (Denmoor); Sites 2, 4 and 5 have employee representative forums without statutory consultation standing. Collective-redundancy obligations engage at 10 or more dismissals within 30 days per establishment, with a 30-day minimum consultation period and notification to the labour authority. Hurdle rate 12% post-tax. All figures are euros, last twelve months unless stated.

---

## 1. Executive summary — one page

**The problem.** Labour cost per picked line is rising 5–6% a year. Error rate at 2.1 per 1,000 lines is concentrated in the twelve accounts that carry 41% of revenue. Picker turnover of 35% both costs money and manufactures the errors. The network runs at 96% of effective capacity in peak week, which means there is currently no slack anywhere to absorb a conversion.

**What the vendor cases actually show.** Both vendors' three-year payback survives only inside their own boundary. Rebuilt to include systems, integration, facility works, dual-running, ramp loss, service escalation and a realistic benefit-capture rate, Vendor A's goods-to-person proposal for Site 1 pays back in **6.5 to 8.0 years at an IRR of roughly 7%**, below hurdle (§6). This is not a criticism of the vendors, who modelled what they were asked to model. It does mean the committee is not choosing between automation and inaction; it is choosing the order.

**Recommendation — Option A, quality-led sequence.**

| Stage | Content | Capital | Sanction point | Realised annual benefit | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** (Months 0–12) | Rungs 0–2 network-wide: slotting, pick-path, rostering, inventory accuracy, scan-verify, check-weigh, print-and-apply, batch/cluster redesign. AMR pilot enablement at Site 2. | **€6.9m** | **Now** | €4.1m | **18–24 months** |
| **Stage 2** (Months 10–30) | AMR fleets under robotics-as-a-service at Sites 2 and 1. Insourcing of returns, kitting and value-added work at Site 1. | €2.3m capital + opex per pick | Gate 2, Month 10 | €5.6m cumulative | 30–36 months |
| **Stage 3** (Months 30–60) | Goods-to-person or cube storage at Site 1 only, if Stage 2 metrics earn it. Site 4 network-role decision at lease break. | €18–24m | Gate 3, Month 30 | To be re-underwritten | 5–6 years on incremental |

Indicative five-year envelope €31–34m, of which **only €9.2m is committed before Gate 3**. Nothing irreversible is bought in the first thirty months.

**Cost of the sequence, stated honestly.** Deferring heavy automation costs roughly €1.3m in year-one compounding labour inflation and about €2.9m across Stages 1–2 in benefit not yet harvested. Against that, Stage 1 delivers €4.1m annually from month nine at a fifth of the capital, releases roughly 7% effective capacity we do not currently have, and rebuilds the inventory and process discipline without which heavy automation fails. Our view is that this is sequencing, not delay — but the committee should see the price of patience, and now it can.

**Workforce.** Gross role reduction of 214 FTE over five years, of which **zero involuntary

# Entering a New Region: Recommended Strategy

**Prepared for discussion at the management meeting — Revision 2**

*Preparation note: this revision reflects comments from colleagues in production, finance and wholesale, and informal input from two of our longest-standing European stockists who buy for Asian clients. Where a view is not yet shared across the group, that is marked. The intention is that the leadership team can confirm or redirect the two framing decisions in §1 before the rest is committed to.*

---

## 1. Two mandates, and which one leads

The brief joins two objectives that behave very differently:

- **Demand mandate** — new customers, new price ceiling, brand legitimacy in a market that will examine our claims closely.
- **Supply mandate** — traceable manufacturing depth, reduced dependence on a single sourcing base, shorter lead times.

Markets that pay well for considered clothing and regions that make it well and affordably are rarely the same place. Our recommendation is therefore **one region, two tracks, deliberately sequenced — demand proof first, supply commitment second.** The reasoning is in §7.

**Guidance requested:** if the leadership team's priority is in fact supply resilience rather than revenue growth, the sequence should invert, and we would want to hear that plainly before Stage 1 spend. Everything downstream depends on it.

---

## 2. Region selection — candidates scored

Six candidates were scored 1–5 against weighted criteria. Weights were agreed with finance and production before scoring, and the working sheet is available.

| Criterion | Weight | Korea | Japan | India | Türkiye (nearshore) | UAE/Gulf | Canada/US PNW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Demonstrated premium apparel spend (behaviour, not intent) | 20% | 5 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 |
| Growth trajectory of target segment | 15% | 4 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| Regulatory clarity on environmental claims | 10% | 4 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 4 |
| Traceable manufacturing depth (fibre→garment) | 20% | 1 | 2 | 5 | 4 | 1 | 1 |
| Digital retail maturity (cheap testing) | 15% | 5 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| Proximity to existing operating capability (low execution risk) | 10% | 3 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 5 |
| Currency stability against EUR cost base | 10% | 3 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 4 |
| **Weighted total** | | **3.55** | **2.85** | **3.75** | **3.00** | **3.15** | **3.35** |

**Recommendation:** **South Korea as the demand beachhead; India as the sourcing and traceability partner.** Together they score highest and, importantly, they do not compete for the same organisational attention — one is a commercial exercise, the other a technical one.

**Why the runners-up lost, in one line each:**

- **Japan** — the market our product philosophy most resembles, and for that reason the hardest to enter: a contracting, deflationary apparel market where the "made to be kept" territory is already held by Muji, Uniqlo (+U/Lemaire), 45R, visvim, Kapital, Nanamica and Snow Peak, with better cost positions and decades of local credibility; the yen's ~30%+ depreciation against the euro since 2021 makes a euro-cost garment read as luxury. **Kept warm as market two, from the same regional hub, from Year 3.**
- **Türkiye / Portugal nearshore** — genuinely superior on lead time and MOQ flexibility, and we should expand nearshore capacity regardless; it does not answer the demand mandate at all.
- **Canada / US PNW** — lowest ambiguity and fastest revenue, no manufacturing contribution, and a crowded field of established sustainable brands.
- **UAE/Gulf** — attractive currency and retail spend; assortment (heavy natural fibres, seasonless) is poorly matched and the segment is thin.
- **Vietnam** — treated with respect, and we would not close the door; on this timetable it is less well matched than India for the reasons in §5.

---

## 3. Competitive map — South Korea

The wedge must be specific against each incumbent, not general.

| Incumbent | Positioning | Approx. RRP band (knit/outerwear) | Our wedge |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Uniqlo / Muji Korea** | Accessible quality, quiet design | €25–70 / €80–150 | Verifiable fibre provenance, repair service, adult fit; we do not compete on price |
| **Kolon FnC — RE;CODE / Nau** | Domestic sustainability leadership, upcycling | €90–200 / €200–400 | Consistent repeatable core range vs. limited-run upcycling; European construction standards |
| **Musinsa-native contemporary brands** (e.g. Amomento, Osoi tier) | Design-led, trend-cycled, strong platform presence | €120–260 | Longevity and take-back; we are not a season-led brand |
| **Patagonia Korea / outdoor-adjacent** | Credible environmental authority | €120–350 | Everyday urban wardrobe rather than technical/outdoor |
| **Imported European "quiet" brands** (Arket, Toteme tier) | European restraint, premium | €120–450 | Sharper price-to-substance ratio, Korean fit blocks, local repair — the imports rarely localise |

**Honest reading:** the segment is contested but not saturated at our specific intersection — *European construction credibility + verifiable traceability + locally graded fit + service after purchase*. The two competitors we cannot outspend (Uniqlo, Kolon) we can out-specify. The Korean contemporary brands we cannot out-design we can outlast.

---

## 4. Product positioning and pricing — with the maths shown

**Lead with the garment; let the ethics be discovered.** Position on material honesty, construction, longevity and fit. Sustainability sits one layer down: verifiable, documented, unmissable to anyone who looks, never the headline. In this market, moralising reads as insecurity about the product.

- Europe (current): *"Clothing that doesn't cost the earth."*
- Korea (proposed): **"Made to be kept."** — repairability, take-back, seasonless colour, Korean fit grading.

**Assortment:** 14–18 SKUs from proven European bestsellers, re-graded. Season one buy ≈ 6,000–9,000 units. Narrow range protects working capital and does brand work through scarcity.

**Localisation that is not cosmetic:** Korean fit blocks (shorter sleeve and torso, narrower shoulder), lighter fabric weights for humid summers, Korean-language care labelling matched to local laundering, Korean sizing nomenclature, and the retail calendar (Korean seasonal cadence and gifting peaks differ materially from ours).

**Landed cost and channel margin — indicative model** (representative organic cotton knit; FX assumption 1 EUR = 1,450 KRW; to be refreshed at Stage 0):

| Line | € per unit |
|---|---|
| Ex-factory cost (current European supply) | 34.00 |
| Freight, insurance, customs clearance | 2.40 |
| Import duty — **0%**, EU-origin under the Korea–EU FTA with origin declaration | 0.00 |
| **Landed cost** | **36.40** |
| Korean RRP incl. 10% VAT (KRW 249,000) | ≈172 |
| Net revenue ex-VAT (DTC) | 156 |

| Channel | Net revenue/unit | Gross margin | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Own DTC (localised site) | €156 | ~70% after payments, last-mile, returns provision | Highest margin, highest CAC |
| Marketplace (Musinsa / 29CM / W Concept, 25–33% commission) | €105–117 | 58–65% | Traffic without CAC; less control of presentation |
| Wholesale to boutiques / department store corners (2.4× markup) | €65 | ~43% | Borrowed credibility; margin cost accepted deliberately |

**Two conclusions the model forces:**

1. **The "hold European price" instruction survives in Korea — and would not have survived in Japan.** Korea–EU FTA duty-free access plus a won that has weakened far less than the yen leaves room to price at European parity (+5–8% to cover local service costs) without becoming a luxury proposition. This is a substantive reason the region ranking changed.
2. **Sourcing from India would *reduce* landed margin on Korea-bound goods**, since India-origin apparel does not enjoy the same duty-free treatment (Korea–India CEPA concessions on apparel are partial). The correct design is therefore: **India-made goods serve European and other markets; Korea is served from EU-origin supply until volumes justify a re-examination.** This resolves, rather than defers, the sell-first-or-source-first question.

**FX policy:** price in won, hold won prices for a full 12 months (frequent repricing is fatal to premium perception), hedge 60–70% of forecast KRW revenue on a 9-month rolling basis, and treat local-currency cost (3PL, repair, marketing, salaries) as the primary structural hedge.

---

## 5. Sourcing — fibre-to-garment, and an MOQ reality check

Our moat is verifiable provenance, so a factory shortlist alone is insufficient. The map we intend to build and audit:

| Tier | What we must see and hold on file |
|---|---|
| **Fibre** | GOTS/organic certification at farm-group level; India holds roughly half of world organic cotton supply — transaction certificates, not assurances |
| **Spinning** | Named mill, GOTS scope certificate, no undeclared blending |
| **Knitting / weaving** | Named mill; **this is the tier we lose if we assemble in a cut-and-sew economy that imports most of its fabric** |
| **Dyeing / finishing** | ZDHC MRSL conformance, water discharge data, energy source |
| **Cut & sew** | SA8000 or Fair Wear; independent audit before first PO |
| **Trims** | Often the weakest link in a claim; documented |
| **Data layer** | GS1-based item-level traceability, built for EU Digital Product Passport obligations arriving under ESPR later this decade |

**MOQ reality check** — the variable that actually decides this:

| Base | Realistic MOQ per style/colour | Match to our 6,000–9,000-unit season |
|---|---|---|
| Vertically integrated Indian suppliers (Tirupur knits; NCR/Bengaluru woven) | 300–600 | **Good fit**; mill and garment tiers under one certificate scope |
| Tier-1 Vietnamese factories serving global sportswear | 2,000–5,000+ | Poor fit at our scale, and fabric largely imported — the mill tier becomes invisible to us |
| Portugal / Türkiye | 150–400 | Excellent flexibility, higher unit cost — retain for European replenishment and newness |

**Recommendation:** qualify **two Indian vertically integrated suppliers** in parallel with the Korean commercial test, place first orders against *European* demand (where EVFTA-style origin logic and our existing customer base already exist), and only then consider Asian-region supply for Asian-region sale. Retain one Portuguese or Turkish partner as the fast-replenishment hedge. Independent audit precedes any purchase order, without exception.

---

## 6. Marketing and channels — named, not generic

**Sequence begins at month 3, after trademark filings are lodged (see §7).**

**Phase A — Credibility (months 3–9), ~€90k**
- 8–12 curated boutiques and one department-store corner test (Hyundai or Shinsegae), chosen because their curation *is* the endorsement.
- **29CM**

|---|---|

| Total FTE | 815 |

| Fully loaded labour cost | €33.4m |
| — of which pick / pack / despatch | €22.9m |
| Cost per picked line (labour only) | €0.369 |
| Mispick / mis-ship rate | 2.1 per 1,000 lines |
| Errors per year | ~130,000 |
| Blended cost per error (credit, return freight, re-pick, admin) | €31 |
| **Direct error cost** | **€4.0m** |
| Picker turnover (annualised) | 35% |

| Network capacity utilisation at peak week | 96% |

1. **The error cost is 17% of the pick labour cost and almost none of it is being managed.** It is also concentrated: 12 accounts representing 41% of revenue absorb 58% of errors, because they order the deepest, most SKU-similar assortments. # Critique — "Automation and Workforce Transition, Revision 1"

## Verdict up front

The document has a good opening instinct and then stops before it does any of the work that was asked for. Four explicit deliverables were requested — degree and sequence of automation per site, the workforce transition mechanics, service-level continuity during conversion, and benefits measurement. **Zero of the four are present.** The draft ends mid-sentence in §2, having spent its length on framing and a single baseline table. Sections 8 and 9 are cross-referenced but do not exist.

Everything below assumes the author intends to continue. The point of the critique is to fix what is wrong in the existing 20% before it propagates into the missing 80%.

---

## 1. Analytical errors in what is present

**a) Double counting between the error line and the turnover line.** "Replacement cost per picker" is defined as including "error tax during ramp" (€4,500 × 196 = €0.9m). The €4.0m direct error cost is calculated from *all* 130,000 errors, which necessarily includes those same ramp-period errors. The two lines overlap by an unstated amount. Either strip the error tax out of replacement cost or present error cost split into steady-state and ramp-attributable. As written, the baseline that the document insists must be "locked and independently attested" contains a known double count.

**b) The error cost is understated in the way that matters most.** The €31 blended cost covers credit, freight, re-pick, admin. The stated business problem is that errors "damage key accounts" — i.e. churn risk on 41% of revenue. That cost is nowhere in the table. A programme whose central argument is "quality leads" has failed to quantify the quality exposure. Add a scenario line: probability-weighted revenue and contribution at risk across the 12 concentrated accounts, even as a range. Done properly, this is likely to dwarf the €4.0m and it is the strongest available justification for the recommended sequence.

**c) A causal claim is asserted, not shown.** "12 accounts … absorb 58% of errors, *because* they order the deepest, most SKU-similar assortments." Plausible, but competing explanations (slotting quality, zone assignment, which shift and which tenure cohort picks those zones, order profile, UoM confusion) carry entirely different remedies. If the real driver is that new hires are disproportionately assigned to the hardest zones, the fix is a rostering rule costing nothing. This needs a root-cause decomposition before it drives capital.

**d) Error taxonomy is missing entirely.** "Mispick / mis-ship" is one blended metric. Wrong SKU, wrong quantity, wrong carton/label and damage have different remedies at wildly different price points — quantity errors are largely solved by check-weighing at a few tens of thousands of euros per line, wrong-SKU by scan-verify, labelling errors by print-and-apply. Without the split, no one can judge whether picking automation is the right instrument at all.

**e) The 96% peak utilisation figure is stated and then abandoned.** It is arguably the single most consequential number in the document: at 96% there is no slack anywhere in the network to absorb a conversion productivity dip, no ability to shift volume between sites during cutover, and no room for growth. It should be driving the sequencing logic and the contingency plan, and it should be paired with a five-year volume and order-profile forecast that does not appear anywhere.

**f) False precision.** €0.369 per line, 62.0m lines, 2.1 per 1,000 — presented to three significant figures with an accompanying admission that none of it is attested. The internal arithmetic does check out (lines × error rate × unit cost, labour ÷ lines, turnover × replacement cost all reconcile, which is to the author's credit), but precision without provenance will be the first thing a sceptical committee member attacks. Add a source-and-confidence column and express the contested figures as ranges.

---

## 2. Missing inputs that make the requested decisions impossible

The brief is fundamentally a **per-site** decision, and there is no site-level data at all. Rev 2 cannot proceed without a five-row table covering, per site:

- Throughput (lines, units, orders, cube), seasonality, and share of the 12 concentrated accounts
- Headcount, tenure distribution, agency/temp proportion, local attrition, absence
- Building constraints — clear height, floor flatness, column grid, dock count, lease term and break, expandable land, power capacity
- Local labour market slack (this is what actually determines whether headcount reduction is humane or catastrophic — and it is the whole point of the "company town" problem)
- Systems state: WMS version, inventory record accuracy, barcoding/GS1 coverage, integration capability
- Union/works council coverage and consultation obligations

Also absent: any capital envelope figure, hurdle rate, or the current state of the vendors' actual numbers. The draft claims a "deliberately sceptical pass over both vendors' business cases" and then shows none of it. A committee needs the **bridge from the vendors' 3-year payback to a defensible one** — line by line: WMS/WES upgrade, integration, facility works, dual-running, ramp-curve productivity loss, spares and service contract escalators, software licences, obsolescence and residual value, and above all the benefit-realisation assumption (vendor cases habitually assume 100% of modelled hours are actually removed from the payroll). My expectation is that this exercise converts 3 years into 5–7 and makes the argument for the recommended sequence far better than rhetoric does.

---

## 3. Substantive disagreements with the positions already taken

**a) The company-town decision is pre-committed and probably wrong.** "Converted late, differently, and toward *more* labour rather than less" is asserted in §1 with no analysis behind it. Two problems. First, if that site is the largest, deferring it strands most of the network benefit and leaves the community's exposure unresolved while the organisation's appetite and capital both decay. Second, "toward more labour" directly contradicts the cost mandate and will read to the committee as sentiment substituting for a plan.

The stronger and more interesting move is the opposite: **automate that site early, under a publicly stated no-involuntary-redundancy commitment for a defined period, and simultaneously insource work to absorb the freed hours** — returns processing, kitting and value-add services, light assembly, currently-outsourced overflow, e-commerce fulfilment for accounts you do not serve today. That converts the community risk into the programme's proof point and reference story rather than its deferred liability. Prolonged uncertainty is usually worse for a town than an early, well-funded, honestly announced transition. Whichever way this lands, it needs to be argued, not declared.

**b) 35% turnover is treated purely as a cost. It is also the transition instrument, and the document has not noticed.** Roughly 196 picker departures a year is natural runoff sufficient to absorb a very large proportion of automation-driven headcount reduction with no layoffs at all — through hiring freezes, agency conversion, red-circling and internal transfer. This reframing should be central to the workforce track, and it creates a genuine tension worth surfacing honestly: the quality programme will *reduce* turnover, which reduces the runoff available for painless downsizing. That trade-off deserves a paragraph and a phasing decision, not silence.

**c) "Quality first, cost later" needs its own cost quantified.** Labour cost is compounding at 5–6% on €22.9m — roughly €1.3m in year one of any delay. Patience is a defensible recommendation but only if the paper prices it and shows the sequence is design, not deferral.

**d) The automation ladder is missing, and with it the capital-lite options.** Nothing yet distinguishes degrees of automation: slotting and pick-path optimisation → scan/voice verification and check-weighing → zone/batch redesign → AMR fleets (low capex, per-unit opex, building-agnostic, scalable, reversible) → goods-to-person shuttle or cube storage (high capex, high commitment, building-dependent) → full AS/RS. Given "capital available but not unlimited" and a competitor's public failure, **robotics-as-a-service and phased AMR deployment are the obvious risk-and-capital structure** — they permit stage-gating, avoid a single irreversible commitment, and preserve the manual fallback. Their absence is the biggest missed innovation in the draft.

**e) The competitor incident is invoked as atmosphere and never used.** It is cited as "an unattributed read … from someone who lived through it" — which is simultaneously the most valuable input available and a governance problem to cite that way in a committee paper. Rev 2 should convert it into an explicit pre-mortem with design rules: big-bang versus zone-by-zone cutover, inventory record accuracy thresholds before go-live, go-live blackout windows around peak, superuser density, retention of manual racking as fallback, single-vendor integration dependency, and who owns the abort decision. Then verify what can be verified from public reporting and drop the hearsay framing.

---

## 4. Structure, tone and format

- The document borrows its architecture and voice wholesale from an unrelated market-entry paper — "Prepared for discussion at…, Revision 1", "Preparation note", "Guidance requested", "one programme, three tracks, sequenced", "Three observations that reorder the priorities", "Where the group does not yet hold a common view, it is marked." The mannerisms are being reused as a substitute for domain-specific thinking. It reads as template, and a warehouse capital committee is a different audience from a brand leadership team.
- The "Guidance requested" paragraph imputes bad faith: *"If the committee's real priority is a headline capital deployment on a three-year payback narrative — for reasons outside operations."* Followed by *"Our view, offered once and then set aside."* This is performative and needlessly antagonising. Replace with a neutral two-option decision frame, each with its own sequence, cost, risk and payback, and let the committee choose on the merits.
- No executive summary, no one-page roadmap, no capital phasing chart, no decision list with dates and owners. A committee paper needs all four.
- Currency is euros with no stated geography, which matters because collective-redundancy law, works council obligations and consultation timelines are jurisdiction-specific and drive the workforce timeline. State the assumption.

---

## 5. What Revision 2 must contain to pass

1. Executive summary with the recommendation, capital envelope, phasing and expected payback range — one page.
2. Corrected baseline: double count removed, source/confidence column, ranges on contested figures, error taxonomy split, account-churn exposure quantified.
3. Five-site profile table (throughput, tenure, building, labour market, systems) and a five-year volume/order-profile forecast.
4. Automation-degree ladder with a per-site verdict and explicit sequence, including the RaaS/AMR capital-lite option and lease-versus-buy.
5. Vendor case teardown: line-by-line bridge from 3-year to realistic payback, with sensitivities and the benefit-realisation assumption made explicit.
6. Workforce transition mechanics: attrition-runoff model, hiring freeze and agency conversion, redeployment map to named new roles with wage grades, retraining partners and vendor certification, severance and bridge-to-retirement terms, tenure-weighted selection criteria, consultation timeline against legal obligations, and the public commitments the company is willing to make and honour.
7. Service continuity plan: pilot zone, dual-running, inventory accuracy gate, peak blackout windows, overflow bridge given 96% utilisation, rollback to manual, named abort authority.
8. Benefits realisation framework: stage gates with kill criteria, leading and lagging metrics, per-line cost, error rate by account, OTIF, robot availability, benefit *capture* rate (hours actually removed from payroll or volume absorbed without hiring), independent attestation, plus account-health and community metrics.
9. Stakeholder and communications sequencing: unions/works councils, local officials, the 12 key accounts, employees, media — who hears what, in what order, with pre-drafted holding lines.
10. Risk register with the competitor-failure modes explicitly mapped to mitigations.

The framing in §1 is worth keeping. Almost nothing else can survive as-is, and the deliverable does not yet exist.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

**Paper for the Operations and Capital Committee — Revision 2**
**Sanction requested: Stage 1 only (€6.9m). Stages 2 and 3 return to this committee at named gates.**

---

### How this revision was prepared

Revision 1 was, quite properly, sent back. It set out a way of thinking about the problem and did not answer the four questions the committee actually asked. This revision answers all four, and in doing so accepts several challenges that were put to us — most importantly on the treatment of our largest site, where the earlier draft substituted a sentiment for a plan. We are grateful for the correction and have reversed the position; the reasoning is set out openly in §7 rather than quietly amended.

The work was done with the five site general managers over four sessions, with HR on tenure and attrition records, with Finance on the baseline and the hurdle test, and with Internal Audit on what can and cannot be attested. Where the group has reached a shared view, the paper says so. Where views still differ — and on two matters they do — the difference is recorded rather than smoothed over, so that the committee decides with the same information the working group has.

**Stated assumptions.** All five sites operate in a single euro-area jurisdiction. Works councils are in place at Site 1 (Halverton) and Site 3 (Denmoor); Sites 2, 4 and 5 have employee representative forums without statutory consultation standing. Collective-redundancy obligations engage at 10 or more dismissals within 30 days per establishment, with a 30-day minimum consultation period and notification to the labour authority. Hurdle rate 12% post-tax. All figures are euros, last twelve months unless stated.

---

## 1. Executive summary — one page

**The problem.** Labour cost per picked line is rising 5–6% a year. Error rate at 2.1 per 1,000 lines is concentrated in the twelve accounts that carry 41% of revenue. Picker turnover of 35% both costs money and manufactures the errors. The network runs at 96% of effective capacity in peak week, which means there is currently no slack anywhere to absorb a conversion.

**What the vendor cases actually show.** Both vendors' three-year payback survives only inside their own boundary. Rebuilt to include systems, integration, facility works, dual-running, ramp loss, service escalation and a realistic benefit-capture rate, Vendor A's goods-to-person proposal for Site 1 pays back in **6.5 to 8.0 years at an IRR of roughly 7%**, below hurdle (§6). This is not a criticism of the vendors, who modelled what they were asked to model. It does mean the committee is not choosing between automation and inaction; it is choosing the order.

**Recommendation — Option A, quality-led sequence.**

| Stage | Content | Capital | Sanction point | Realised annual benefit | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** (Months 0–12) | Rungs 0–2 network-wide: slotting, pick-path, rostering, inventory accuracy, scan-verify, check-weigh, print-and-apply, batch/cluster redesign. AMR pilot enablement at Site 2. | **€6.9m** | **Now** | €4.1m | **18–24 months** |
| **Stage 2** (Months 10–30) | AMR fleets under robotics-as-a-service at Sites 2 and 1. Insourcing of returns, kitting and value-added work at Site 1. | €2.3m capital + opex per pick | Gate 2, Month 10 | €5.6m cumulative | 30–36 months |
| **Stage 3** (Months 30–60) | Goods-to-person or cube storage at Site 1 only, if Stage 2 metrics earn it. Site 4 network-role decision at lease break. | €18–24m | Gate 3, Month 30 | To be re-underwritten | 5–6 years on incremental |

Indicative five-year envelope €31–34m, of which **only €9.2m is committed before Gate 3**. Nothing irreversible is bought in the first thirty months.

**Cost of the sequence, stated honestly.** Deferring heavy automation costs roughly €1.3m in year-one compounding labour inflation and about €2.9m across Stages 1–2 in benefit not yet harvested. Against that, Stage 1 delivers €4.1m annually from month nine at a fifth of the capital, releases roughly 7% effective capacity we do not currently have, and rebuilds the inventory and process discipline without which heavy automation fails. Our view is that this is sequencing, not delay — but the committee should see the price of patience, and now it can.

**Workforce.** Gross role reduction of 214 FTE over five years, of which **zero involuntary
